outputs.L1:
Yes, injured Woman! Rise, assert thy right!  
Woman, too long degraded, scorned, oppressed—  
O born to rule in partial Law’s despite,  
Resume thy native empire o’er the breast!

Go forth, arrayed in panoply divine,  
That angel pureness which admits no stain;  
Go, bid proud Man his boasted rule resign,  
And kiss the golden sceptre of thy reign.

Go, gird thyself with grace; collect thy store  
Of bright artillery, glancing from afar:  
Soft, melting tones—thy thundering cannon’s roar;  
Blushes and fears—thy magazine of war.

Thy rights are empire: urge no meaner claim—  
Felt, not defined, and, if debated, lost;  
Like sacred mysteries, which, withheld from fame  
And shunning discussion, are revered the most.

Try all that wit and art suggest to bend  
Thy imperial foe’s stubborn knee;  
Make treacherous Man thy subject, not thy friend:  
Thou mayst command, but never canst be free.

Awe the licentious, and restrain the rude;  
Soften the sullen; clear the cloudy brow.  
Be thy favours sued for more than princes’ gifts—  
She hazards all who will the least allow.

But hope not, courted idol of mankind,  
Upon this proud eminence secure to stay;  
Subduing and subdued, thou soon shalt find  
Thy coldness soften and thy pride give way.

Then, then abandon each ambitious thought;  
Conquest or rule shall feebly move thy heart.  
In Nature’s school, taught by her gentle maxims,  
Learn that separate rights are lost in mutual love.
outputs.L2:
Rise, wronged woman, and claim what is yours. For far too long you have endured humiliation, contempt, and oppression. Though biased laws deny your authority, you were made to govern the human heart; reclaim that natural dominion.

Step forward clothed in heavenly armor, protected by an angelic innocence untouched by corruption. Order arrogant man to surrender the power of which he boasts and to bow before the golden symbol of your sovereignty.

Equip yourself with grace and gather your shining weapons: let gentle, tender speech serve as the blast of cannon, while modest blushes and anxious reserve supply your arsenal. Demand nothing less than dominion as your right. Such authority must be felt rather than precisely explained, for argument destroys it. Like sacred secrets, it commands greatest reverence when kept from public exposure and spared debate.

Use every device that intelligence and skill can invent to force your proud opponent to kneel. Turn deceitful man into your subject rather than your companion. You may rule him, though you can never thereby gain freedom.

Intimidate the immoral, restrain the uncivilized, calm the gloomy, and brighten troubled faces. Make your approval more eagerly sought than the rewards of kings, for the woman who yields even a little puts everything at risk.

Yet do not imagine, adored by humanity, that you can remain forever secure upon this lofty height. Even while conquering, you will also be conquered: your reserve will gradually thaw, and your pride will surrender.

At that moment, give up every dream of ambition. Victory and authority will cease to stir your heart. Nature, teaching through her gentle principles, will show you that separate claims to rights disappear when two people are joined in mutual love.
outputs.L3:
The poem urges women to resist their degradation and reclaim the influence that properly belongs to them. Rather than presenting female power as political or institutional authority, it locates women’s strength in qualities such as purity, grace, wit, and emotional appeal. These qualities are portrayed as weapons through which women can compel men to relinquish their dominance and submit to female influence.

At the same time, the poem defines women’s rights as a subtle, intuitive kind of empire. This authority is most effective when it is exercised indirectly; once it is openly debated, formally asserted, or precisely defined, it begins to lose its power. Women are therefore advised not to pursue equality through friendship or abstract freedom, but to command men through personal and moral influence. Their role is to restrain male rudeness, violence, and immorality, thereby refining social behavior.

Yet the poem ultimately moves beyond the language of conquest and authority. The struggle for power gives way to reciprocal love, in which neither sex seeks to rule the other. In genuine affection, separate claims to rights, dominance, and ambition cease to matter, as both women and men find fulfillment in mutual devotion.
outputs.L4:
The poem responds to women’s oppression by challenging the assumption that power exists only in formal laws, public institutions, and openly debated political rights. In an ironic voice, it urges women to recognize the influence they already exercise over men through beauty, moral purity, intelligence, wit, and emotional insight. These qualities are presented almost as weapons by which women might reverse the existing hierarchy and make men submit to them. Yet the poem does not seriously propose replacing male domination with female domination. Instead, its exaggerated language exposes the limitations of any struggle based on one sex ruling the other.

By the conclusion, the poem moves beyond rivalry and competing claims to authority. It suggests that domination, whoever exercises it, cannot produce genuine freedom, because mastery always depends on inequality and submission. When love is mutual, the distinction between ruler and ruled loses its meaning: each person gives affection freely and receives it in return. The poem therefore transforms its apparent argument for feminine power into a broader vision of reciprocity. Rather than endorsing either male authority or female control, it imagines a relationship in which separate claims to power dissolve through shared love, equality, and emotional interdependence.
outputs.L5:
**Yes, Woman, Law**

“Yes” is a powerful word when spoken freely. For every woman, it should represent choice, dignity, and control over her own life. The law has a responsibility to protect that freedom—not only in principle, but in practice.

A just society ensures that women can say yes to education, employment, leadership, marriage, or motherhood without discrimination or coercion. It must also respect their right to say no. Through equal rights, fair enforcement, and meaningful access to justice, the law can transform freedom from an ideal into a lived reality.

When a woman’s voice is heard and her choices are protected, equality becomes more than a promise. It becomes the law.

counterfactuals.output:
## “The Rights of Woman”  
### Anna Laetitia Barbauld

Yes, injured Woman! rise, assert thy right!  
Woman! too long degraded, scorned, opprest;  
O born to rule in partial Law’s despite,  
Resume thy native empire o’er the breast!

Go forth arrayed in panoply divine;  
That angel pureness which admits no stain;  
Go, bid proud Man his boasted rule resign,  
And kiss the golden sceptre of thy reign.

Go, gird thyself with grace; collect thy store  
Of bright artillery glancing from afar;  
Soft melting tones thy thundering cannon’s roar,  
Blushes and fears thy magazine of war.

Thy rights are empire: urge no meaner claim,  
Felt, not defined, and if debated, lost;  
Like sacred mysteries, which withheld from fame,  
Shunning discussion, are revered the most.

Try all that wit and art suggest to bend  
Of thy imperial foe the stubborn knee;  
Make treacherous Man thy subject, not thy friend;  
Thou mayst command, but never canst be free.

Awe the licentious, and restrain the rude;  
Soften the sullen, clear the cloudy brow:  
Be, more than princes’ gifts, thy favours sued;—  
She hazards all, who will the least allow.

But hope not, courted idol of mankind,  
On this proud eminence secure to stay;  
Subduing and subdued, thou soon shalt find  
Thy coldness soften, and thy pride give way.

Then, then, abandon each ambitious thought,  
Conquest or rule thy heart shall feebly move,  
In Nature’s school, by her soft maxims taught,  
That separate rights are lost in mutual love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
